paper_title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

sections.content: 1. Introduction Understanding scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/PINE Understanding scene requires both geometry and semantics [17, 75]. Geometry describes where each surface lies and how it is oriented, and semantics describes which surfaces form one object. Specialist models [68, 82] now recover each part from single image with high accuracy. The Depth Anything [30, 71, 72] and MoGe [24, 58, 59] series predict depth, point map and normals. Diffusion estimators such as Marigold [19, 42] and Lotus [14] predict detailed depth and surface normals, and GenPercept [64] and E2E-FT [37] reduce them to one sampling step. The SAM series [21, 49] segments any object under prompt, and gen2seg [20] colors every instance with generative model. None of these models predicts all three maps in one forward pass. full parse of one image chains geometry model and segmentation model. Their latencies and memory add up, and their maps do not share one camera. Pointmap models [24, 30, 33, 45, 59] can take the intrinsics, whereas diffusion normal estimators [11, 14, 19, 37, 73] take the image alone, even when the intrinsics are given. Generalist models such as 4M [40], Unified-IO [35], DICEPTION [78] and OneDiffusion [25] cast multiple tasks into one network. They do not remove the cost: DICEPTION runs one forward pass per map, and OneDiffusion needs multiple sampling steps for each map. direct solution is one Diffusion Transformer that predicts all maps together in one step. Yet Diffusion Transformer [43] is designed for RGB images. The three maps break three of its assumptions. The instance map has no fixed target, because it is correct under any permutation of its colors. The point map places each depth along the camera ray of its pixel, but transformer indexes its tokens by pixel [43]. full view and zoomed crop then give one scene point two positions. The normals and the instance map are constant over surfaces and objects, but attention recovers this grouping from the tokens alone. In practice, the attention of patch spreads over other objects. Based on these observations, we present PINE, onestep Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the normals and the instance map in one forward pass, as Fig. 1 shows. PINE revises these three assumptions. For the target, PINE represents each map as token stream. The geometry streams follow flow matching at their own timesteps, while the instance stream regresses its map with clustering loss. stream mask keeps the instance stream apart from the geometry noise. For the position, the cameraaware ray encoding positions the tokens of every stream by the rays of one camera. When the intrinsics are unknown, default camera takes their place. For the grouping, grounding attention writes the affinity of DINOv3 features [54] into the attention logits of the normal and instance streams. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We present PINE, one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer. One forward pass replaces one specialist model per map and multiple sampling steps of diffusion estimators. We introduce camera-aware ray encoding, which positions tokens by camera rays whether or not intrinsics are given, and grounding attention, which gives the normal and instance streams the grouping of their pixels. PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals, and it exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1% of its training images. It runs 5.7 times faster than MoGe-3 combined with SAM. 2. Related Work Monocular Geometry Estimation. MiDaS [47, 48] and Depth Anything [71, 72] train on mixed or large unlabeled data to predict affine-invariant depth. DUSt3R [60] regresses point maps directly, and MoGe [24, 58, 59] predicts affine-invariant point maps from single image. Without intrinsics, the field of view is ambiguous. Metric3D [74], UniDepth [44, 45], Depth Pro [3], DA3 [30] and FoundationGeo [33] estimate the intrinsics or take them as input. DSINE [1] feeds per-pixel ray directions to normal estimator. All of these models index their features by pixels and predict geometry only. GTA [39] and PRoPE [28] encode the relative cameras of multiple views in attention, whereas PINE positions the tokens of one image by their rays. Diffusion for Dense Prediction. Marigold [19] fine-tunes pretrained latent diffusion model [16, 51] into zero-shot depth estimator. GeoWizard [11], StableNormal [73] and Marigold V2 [42] extend this recipe to normals. FE2E [56] starts from an image editing model. GeoNeXt [69] starts from video generative model and predicts depth and normals as the next frames. GenPercept [64], Lotus [14] and E2E-FT [37] reduce the multiple sampling steps of these estimators to one deterministic step. TransNormal-2 [27] corrects the decoding errors of the autoencoder at object boundaries with pixel-space losses and refinement module. PPD [65], PointDiT [66] and Lapis [32] avoid the detail loss of the autoencoder by denoising in pixel space [29]. Each of these estimators predicts one or two geometric maps, whereas PINE predicts all three maps in one step.

sections.content: segmentation Instance Segmentation. has moved from closed label sets [6, 15] to class-agnostic entities [36]. SimpleClick [34] segments the object under click. The SAM series [21, 49] accepts any prompt and scales this ability with large mask corpus. TokenCut [63], Deep Spectral Methods [38] and CutLER [61] group pixels into objects by the affinities of self-supervised features [41, 54]. gen2seg [20] fine-tunes generative model [51] to color every instance with clustering loss [9]. PINE predicts instances as one stream of geometry model and writes the affinity of DINOv3 features into its attention. Omni Models for Dense Prediction. Multi-task networks such as UberNet [23] and Omnidata [10] share one backbone across geometric and semantic tasks. Taskonomy [75] measures how these tasks transfer. Generalist models cast multiple tasks into one interface, such as images in Painter [62] and token sequences in 4M [40] and Unified-IO [35]. DICEPTION [78] trains one diffusion model for all tasks but runs one forward pass per task. GenCeption [57] turns video generation model into one perception model, where text prompt selects the task. UniDiffuser [2] and OneDiffusion [25] give each modality or view its own timestep, so that any of them can condition the others over multiple sampling steps. PINE is an omni model of different form: each map is token stream, each geometry stream has its own timestep, and one forward pass gives all maps. Figure 2. Overview of PINE. The point, normal and instance streams embed their maps with the frozen DINOv3 features and pass through DiT blocks as one sequence. In attention, the stream mask decides which streams interact, ray positions encode the intrinsics and grounding attention adds the DINOv3 affinity. Each stream decodes its own map, and one step at inference gives all three maps. 3. Results on Surface Normals. PINE-H has the best average rank of all methods in Tab. 2. Its largest gain is on Sintel, where it reaches mean angular error of 25.6 against 26.4 for MoGe-3, the second-best method. It also raises the Sintel accuracy within 11.25 from 29.1% to 32.5%. PINE learns normals from only 139K synthetic images, while MoGe-3 trains on more than 8.9M frames. With intrinsics, PINE-H lowers its error further on all four datasets. Figure 5 shows the normals of PINE-H and baselines. Results on Instances. PINE-H exceeds SAM on large COCO objects and DRAM by 17.6 and 10.7 mIoU in Tab. 3. It also outperforms gen2seg, diffusion-based instance model, on every benchmark. PINE learns instances from only 87K images, while SAM trains on 11M images with 1.1B masks. This shows that instances can be learned as an additional stream of geometry model, without large mask corpus. On small COCO objects, PINE-H trails SAM with 9.2 against 57.2 mIoU, since small object covers only few patches. Figure 5 shows that PINE-H gives more complete masks of large objects than gen2seg. The point maps, the depth and the normals use the benchmarks of Sec. 4.1, and the instances use COCOexc and DRAM. Camera-Aware Ray Encoding. In Tab. 5, without the encoding, intrinsics have no effect, and Relp stays at 5.05 in both settings. With the encoding, intrinsics reduce Relp from 4.82 to 3.94 and the mean angular error from 18.23 to 17.81. Without intrinsics, the encoding still reduces Relp from 5.05 to 4.82. We split the error of each point into lateral part εxy and depth part εz. Averaged over the valid pixels with intrinsics, the encoding reduces εxy from 2.28 to 1.27, but εz only from 3.22 to 2.95. Figure 6 illustrates this split on one image row. The gap in lateral error grows with the distance to the principal point, where wrong focal length moves point the most. During training, Relp with intrinsics stalls near 5.0 without the encoding but keeps dropping to 3.94 with it. Stream Mask. Implementation Details This section complements Secs. 3.4 and 4.1 of the main paper with the full training and inference setup. Table 7 lists the training data. The geometry streams train on the four synthetic datasets, and the instance stream also trains on the instance labels of EntitySeg and ADE20K. On Hypersim, the instance loss uses only the scenes with at least 10 annotated objects, as in gen2seg [20], which leaves 87K images with instance labels. We remove the 555 EntitySeg images that come from COCO val2017, so that no test image of COCOexc enters training. Tables 8 to 10 list the model sizes, the training hyperparameters and the inference settings. A.1. Training Losses The loss weights in Eq. (9) are λrel = 0.1, λgrad = 0.5 and λinst = 0.02. The point-map target xp is normalized for shift and scale as in PointDiT [66]. In Eq. (10), the sky pixels add the same error, averaged separately and weighted by λsky = 0.01. The gradient loss Lgrad is the multi-scale gradient matching loss of MiDaS [47] on the log-depth error, which sharpens depth edges. The normal loss Lsink follows Marigold V2 [42]: inside every 5 5 window, Sinkhorn plan matches the predicted normals to the target normals before the L1 error is taken. The instance loss Linst follows gen2seg [20], which adapts the discriminative loss of [9]. It pulls the predicted colors of every instance to their mean, pushes all other pixels away from that mean, pushes the means of different instances apart and pulls the background to black. Given that it uses the instance ids only to group pixels, the loss ignores which color an instance takes. A.2. Timesteps and Intrinsics Table 7. Training data.
